definition_verbatim: (With respect to terminology, SOF are regular troops trained to fight irregularly.)
author: Gray, Colin S.
source_MLA: Gray, Colin S. "Handfuls of Heroes on Desperate Ventures: When Do Special Operations Succeed?" Parameters 29.1 (1999): 2-24.

definition_verbatim: special operations forces offer the prospect of a favorably disproportionate return on military investment... SOF provide the possibility of a range of precisely conducted military activities more extensive than that reliably feasible for regular warriors conducting regular operations.
author: Gray, Colin S.
source_MLA: Gray, Colin S. "Handfuls of Heroes on Desperate Ventures." Parameters 29.1 (1999): 2-24.

definition_verbatim: that class of military (or paramilitary) actions that fall outside the realm of conventional warfare during their respective time periods.
author: Arquilla, John (q. in Gray)
source_MLA: Quoted in Gray 1999 from John Arquilla, From Troy to Entebbe (1996), pp. xv-xvi.

definition_verbatim: they are elite warriors, after all--the trouble is that they are few in number
author: Gray, Colin S.
source_MLA: Gray, Colin S. "Handfuls of Heroes." Parameters 29.1 (1999).

definition_verbatim: Special Operation Forces are organizations containing specially selected personnel that are organized, equipped and trained to conduct high-risk, high value special operations to achieve military, political, economic or informational objectives by using special and unique operational methodologies in hostile, denied or politically sensitive areas to achieve desired tactical, operational and/or strategic effects in times of peace, conflict or war.
author: CANSOFCOM (q. in Horn)
source_MLA: Quoted in Bernd Horn, "The Strategic Utility of SOF," Canadian Military Journal 14.4 (2014): 66-70; from CANSOFCOM, An Overview (DND, 2008), p.7.

definition_verbatim: special men, special training and special missions
author: Horn, Bernd
source_MLA: Bernd Horn, "The Strategic Utility of SOF," Canadian Military Journal 14.4 (2014): 66-70.

definition_verbatim: the word commando meant a body of burghers called out for military service, usually on a more or less temporary basis... It corresponded most closely, therefore, to the English term militia. The commando was not the individual burgher, but the military unit of which he was a member.
author: Dobbie, Elliott V. K.
source_MLA: Dobbie, Elliott V. K. "The Word 'Commando'." American Speech 19.2 (1944): 81-90.

definition_verbatim: In World War II, a Commando is a unit of Special Service troops, roughly corresponding in size to a battalion, trained for combined operations.
author: Dobbie, Elliott V. K.
source_MLA: Dobbie, Elliott V. K. "The Word 'Commando'." American Speech 19.2 (1944): 81-90.

definition_verbatim: despite the fact that special operations forces in NATO countries have different titles ("Special Operations Forces" /the USA, Great Britain, France/, "Special Forces" /FRG/, "Special Designation Forces" /Turkey/), they carry out specific functional tasks which are described below.
author: Sliusarenko, Andrii
source_MLA: Sliusarenko, Andrii. "Conceptual Organizational and Functional Models of the Army SOF in the Leading NATO Countries." UR Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences 1(6) (2018): 75-86.

definition_verbatim: foreign analysts consider Special Operations Forces as a "third force" along with nuclear weapons and conventional forces.
author: Safonov (q. in Sliusarenko)
source_MLA: Quoted in Sliusarenko 2018 from Safonov 2000, p.7.

definition_verbatim: The Special Forces group's original mission focused on unconventional warfare-working with indigenous forces to overthrow a hostile government-along with long-range reconnaissance and sabotage operations behind enemy lines.
author: Johnson, Matthew
source_MLA: Johnson, Matthew. "The Growing Relevance of SOF in U.S. Military Strategy." Comparative Strategy 25.4 (2006): 273-296.

definition_verbatim: the toughest, smartest, most secretive, fittest, best-equipped and consistently lethal killers in the U.S. [or any other] military.
author: Walker, William (q. in Horn)
source_MLA: Quoted in Bernd Horn, "When Cultures Collide," Canadian Military Journal 5.3 (2004): 3-16; from W. Walker, Toronto Star, 20 Oct 2001.

definition_verbatim: specially selected, specially trained, specially equipped, and given special missions and support.
author: Clancy, Tom (q. in Horn)
source_MLA: Quoted in Horn 2004 from Tom Clancy, Special Forces (2001), p.3.

definition_verbatim: specially organized, trained and equipped military and paramilitary forces that conduct special operations to achieve military, political, economic or informational objectives by generally unconventional means in hostile, denied or politically sensitive areas.
author: Adams, Thomas K. (q. in Horn)
source_MLA: Quoted in Horn 2004 from Thomas K. Adams, US SOF in Action (1998), p.7.

definition_verbatim: SOF can be broken down into roughly three tiers that correspond both to the rigour of the selection standards and to the role equated with each level... 'Tier One' SOF consists of primarily 'black operations' or counter terrorism... 'Tier Two'... high value tasks such as Strategic Reconnaissance and Unconventional Warfare... 'Tier Three', consists of those units, such as the American Rangers... whose primary mission is Direct Action... Generally, units below this line are not considered SOF.
author: Horn, Bernd
source_MLA: Bernd Horn, "When Cultures Collide," Canadian Military Journal 5.3 (2004): 3-16.

definition_verbatim: an almost universally observed characteristic of elite units is their lack of formal discipline - and sometimes a lack of substantive discipline as well.
author: Cohen, Eliot (q. in Horn)
source_MLA: Quoted in Horn 2004 from Eliot Cohen, Commandos and Politicians, p.74.

definition_verbatim: Members of SF often boil UW down to any effort in which they work 'by, through, and with' indigenous forces. From an SF perspective, the goal of UW is to help win a war by working with-as opposed to neutralizing or fighting around-local populations.
author: Simons, Anna; Tucker, David
source_MLA: Simons, Anna, and David Tucker. "United States SOF and the War on Terrorism." Small Wars & Insurgencies 14.1 (2003): 77-91.

definition_verbatim: A special operations force is a group of intensely committed soldiers that receives special training to employ highly developed skills and its unique experiences to execute, most of the time secretly and covertly, sharply defined missions not normally undertaken by regular forces.
author: Lambakis, Steven
source_MLA: Lambakis, Steven. "'Forty selected men can shake the world': The contributions of special operations to victory." Comparative Strategy 13.2 (1994): 211-221.

definition_verbatim: All special operations forces share certain characteristics... special operations forces can be identified by their flexibility, versatility, adaptability, responsiveness, durability, ingenuity, and capacity to act independently of other military forces.
author: Lambakis, Steven
source_MLA: Lambakis, Steven. Comparative Strategy 13.2 (1994): 211-221.

definition_verbatim: special operations forces are intended to perform special operations. They are not simply elite infantry possessing above-average skills and endurance levels. Regardless of the country or the historical moment, there are intrinsic or constitutional differences between special operations and regular forces.
author: Lambakis, Steven
source_MLA: Lambakis, Steven. Comparative Strategy 13.2 (1994): 211-221.

definition_verbatim: Commando operations in the sense of self-contained acts of war mounted by self-sufficient forces operating within enemy territory are as old as warfare itself.
author: Thomas, David
source_MLA: Thomas, David. "The Importance of Commando Operations in Modern Warfare 1939-82." Journal of Contemporary History 18.4 (1983): 689-717.

term_raw: US Army Special Forces / UW [Thomas q. US doctrine]
definition_verbatim: In 1952, the US Army Special Forces were established for the purpose of waging what the army defined as 'unconventional warfare' in the rear... this form of warfare encompassed guerrilla warfare, escape and evasion, psychological warfare, and subversion. Thus, it had essentially nothing to do with commando operations in the proper sense.
author: Thomas, David (q. US Army doctrine)
source_MLA: Thomas, David. Journal of Contemporary History 18.4 (1983): 689-717.

term_raw: LRPG not a commando unit [Thomas, boundary]
definition_verbatim: the Long Range Penetration Group (LRPG), a large, independent raiding force, which operated on a self-contained basis behind Japanese lines... nor can this force be regarded as a commando unit in the strict sense.
author: Thomas, David
source_MLA: Thomas, David. Journal of Contemporary History 18.4 (1983): 689-717.

term_raw: special operations [Deruelle, by mission not operators]
definition_verbatim: The difference between these special operations and 'regular warfare' (battles, sieges) lay neither in numbers nor in the specialisation of soldiers, but in missions characterised by limited aims, surprise, tricks, stratagems, initiative taken at low levels of command, and constant adaptation.
author: Deruelle, Benjamin
source_MLA: Deruelle, Benjamin. "The sixteenth-century antecedents of special operations 'small war'." Small Wars & Insurgencies 25.4 (2014): 754-766.

definition_verbatim: a 'party' is 'a unit of soldiers that one sends to plunder, or to reconnoitre and ravage the enemy country'.
author: Richelet, Pierre (q. in Deruelle)
source_MLA: Quoted in Deruelle 2014 from Pierre Richelet, Dictionnaire Francois (1680).

definition_verbatim: a detachment is recognised a 'parti' if it has a 'written order from the commander, and if it counts at least... twenty foot soldiers or fifteen horsemen, or else they are considered brigands'.
author: Furetiere, Antoine (q. in Deruelle)
source_MLA: Quoted in Deruelle 2014 from Antoine de Furetiere, Dictionnaire Universel.
